newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Quaker posts loss, chairman to step down.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Quaker posts loss, chairman to step down.

text.p: Quaker Oats Co. Wednesday posted a staggering first quarter loss of $1.1 billion after taking a hit on the sale of its Snapple beverage business, and said it was seeking a replacement for Chairman William Smithburg.
Smithburg, who plans to step down after 16 years as chairman and chief executive officer, has been criticized for purchasing Snapple in December 1994 in a $1.8 billion deal.

"There has been a buzz about it for some time," CS First Boston analyst Michael Mauboussin said of Smithburg's plan to retire soon after a successor is named. "Clearly with the whole Snapple situation, it makes a lot of sense."

Quaker took a one-time charge of $1.14 billion for Snapple, which posted operating losses in 1995 and 1996. Snapple is being sold for $300 million to Triarch Cos. With another $250 million in tax benefits, the total cash value of the Snapple deal is $550 million.
The company, whose products include oatmeal, Rice a Roni, and Gatorade sports drinks, had said in March when it announced the deal that it would take the charge for the Snapple sale.

Smithburg said in a conference call that a search for a successor inside and outside the company began this week, adding he expects it will be a "matter of months" before a replacement is named. After a transition period, Smithburg said he planned to retire.
"This is not a long-term thing," he added.

Excluding the Snapple charge, Quaker said it earned $34.2 million, or 24 cents a share, in the first quarter, up from $32.2 million, or 22 cents a share, a year earlier, which was in line with the company's earlier projection.
Sales declined to $1.20 billion from $1.22 billion. Excluding divested business, sales were up 5 percent.
Quaker also said it might sell more non-core businesses as part of a plan to reduce costs, repurchase shares and focus on its core businesses. It did not identify the units.
Analysts, however, said they expect Quaker to sell its Latin American canned fish and pasta businesses, as well as a U.S. food service coffee operation.
Quaker said it will continue to focus on grain-based businesses and its Gatorade sports drink going forward.
The company also plans to take $50 million to $100 million in pretax restructuring charges by year-end as it realign its businesses.
Commenting on the first quarter, Smithburg said results of the core businesses were strong. "We're pleased with 9 percent earnings growth from ongoing businesses ...," he said in a statement.
Quaker said ready-to-eat cereal volume grew 27 percent, which outpaced the rest of the industry.
"At the same time, U.S. Gatorade reported 15 percent volume growth, and our U.S. hot cereals grew 4 percent," Smithburg said.

Worldwide foods operating income fell to $78.0 million in the quarter from $99.9 million, excluding divested businesses and a gain. The decline was due to an average 15 percent price cut on U.S. ready-to-eat cereals and greater advertising and merchandising spending.
Operating income at Quaker's U.S. and Canadian foods unit fell 22 percent to $77.2 million, while operating income from international food operations slid to $800,000 from $900,000.
Worldwide earnings from Gatorade sports drinks soared 231 percent to $34.4 million.
Quaker also said it will resume share repurchases, which it suspended in the summer of 1994.
Quaker stock rose $1.625 to $39.875 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
